title: Toxic Resilience: What High-Achieving Women Get Wrong About Strength
guestBio: Dr. Katie Pritchett is a neuroscientist, leadership strategist, and executive coach whose work helps leaders understand how the brain shapes the way we lead, decide, and build relationships. She is the author of By Design: Leadership Reframed Through Neuroscience and co-host of the Higher Downloads podcast. Dr. Pritchett's recognize, rewire, rebuild framework gives high-achieving women a science-backed path from survival mode to intentional, sustainable leadership.
excerpt: Neuroscientist and executive coach Dr. Katie Pritchett joins Aimee to name the pattern draining high-achieving women dry: toxic resilience. If "I'm fine, I can handle it" is your default setting, this conversation will finally give language to what's been living underneath it.
metaDescription: Neuroscientist Dr. Katie Pritchett breaks down toxic resilience — why high-achieving women mistake pushing through for strength, and how to rewire it.
keyTakeaways: Toxic resilience is the pattern of overriding your own needs so consistently that you stop recognizing them as needs at all — and it often looks like strength from the outside.
Pushing through without recovering, learning, or changing isn't resilience — it's the same motion on repeat, and your body is keeping score.
Healthy perseverance leaves you tired but still intact; unhealthy endurance quietly excludes you from your own life.
Your nervous system equates 'familiar' with 'safe,' which means rewiring doesn't happen through thinking — it happens through doing something different, repeatedly.
Functioning can feel safer than feeling, but that trade-off comes at a significant cost to your leadership, your relationships, and your health.
You cannot access empathy, creativity, or sound judgment when your nervous system is in a state of hijack — regulation isn't a luxury, it's a leadership requirement.
Women redefine strength not by carrying more, but by building the kind of community where they don't have to carry everything alone.

guestQuiz.description: Dr. Katie Pritchett built a quiz to help you identify the pattern that's quietly draining you — and what to do about it.

content:
There is a version of strength that looks incredible from the outside — and quietly hollows you out from within. You show up. You deliver. You handle it. And when someone asks how you're doing, you say "I'm fine" before the question has even finished landing. That's not weakness. That's a pattern. And in this episode of The Manage Her® Podcast, neuroscientist and executive coach Dr. Katie Pritchett gives it a name: toxic resilience.

The Introduction That Changed Everything

Before Aimee and Katie dive into the science, they open with something that sets the tone for the entire conversation: the power of a single, thoughtful introduction. One connection made through this show didn't just add a contact to Katie's network — it catalyzed the completion of her manuscript and sparked a creative collaboration that wove two books together. Great things don't happen in isolation. That truth, woven throughout this episode, is more than a motivational phrase. It's the lived proof that who you allow into your orbit directly shapes what becomes possible for you.

This is also a love letter to what happens when women genuinely open doors for each other — not performatively, not strategically, but because they believe in the work and the person behind it.

What "Book Midwives" Taught Katie About Witnessing

Katie introduces the concept of "book midwives" — the people who witness your creative and intellectual labor and hold space for it to come to life. It's a metaphor that extends far beyond publishing. Every big, meaningful thing you're building needs witnesses. It needs people who know what you're attempting, who hold the vision with you when you can't hold it alone, and who remind you that starting imperfectly is still starting. You don't need a perfect circle. You need an honest one.

Cultivating Human Potential in the Age of AI

As AI reshapes the professional landscape, Katie argues that the most irreplaceable work — the most human work — is the cultivation of human potential. The ability to read the room, regulate your own nervous system, build trust, and lead with genuine presence: these are not skills that can be automated. They are the competitive advantage of tomorrow's leaders, and they require the kind of self-awareness that many high-achieving women have been trained to skip.

"Tell me who you walk with and I'll tell you who you are." Your community doesn't just reflect your values — it shapes your ceiling. The people you surround yourself with either expand your sense of what's possible or quietly confirm the limits you've already accepted.

Naming the Pattern: What Toxic Resilience Actually Is

Here's where the conversation shifts — and where you may feel something click. Katie defines toxic resilience as the ability to override your own needs so consistently, and so effectively, that you stop recognizing them as needs at all. It doesn't announce itself. It accumulates quietly, beneath every "I've got it," every skipped lunch, every meeting you sat through while your body was screaming for rest.

The insidious part? Pushing through got you praised. It got you promoted. It earned you the reputation of being the one who handles things. So your brain learned that overriding your needs was not just acceptable — it was the path to belonging and success. Resilience, in that context, stopped being a skill and became a survival strategy.

Resilience without recovery isn't strength. It's the same motion on repeat — and your body is keeping score.

Healthy Perseverance vs. Unhealthy Endurance

Katie draws a distinction that deserves to be written somewhere you'll see it every day. Healthy perseverance leaves you tired but still intact — still connected to yourself, still growing, still learning from the hard stretch. Unhealthy endurance excludes you from your own life. You're present in body and absent in everything else. You stop feeling the things that are supposed to tell you something. And here's what makes this particularly dangerous for high-achievers: functioning can feel safer than feeling. The task list is manageable. The emotions are not. So you choose the task list, and you call it productivity.

Why Your Nervous System Chooses Familiar Over Optimal

From a neuroscience standpoint, this pattern isn't a character flaw — it's a wiring issue. Your nervous system doesn't ask "is this good for me?" It asks "is this familiar?" Familiar registers as safe. New, better, more aligned choices register as threat — even when you consciously want them. This is why insight alone doesn't create change. You can know something is true and still not be able to act on it, because your nervous system hasn't caught up to your intellect yet.

Rewiring happens in the doing, not the thinking. Every time you choose differently — every time you honor a need instead of overriding it, every time you ask for support instead of white-knuckling through — you are building new neural pathways. It is not dramatic. It is not instant. But it is how change actually works.

The Recognize, Rewire, Rebuild Framework

Katie's framework gives you a practical on-ramp: recognize the patterns you've been living inside, rewire the nervous system responses that keep you looping, and rebuild the life and leadership that reflect who you're choosing to become — not who you learned to survive as. Living by default means running on old code. Living by design means you get to author what comes next.

You are not broken. You are not behind. You are someone who was praised for a pattern that cost more than it paid — and now you have language for it. That's where the redesign begins.
